A prayer for protection throughout life (verses 1–13)

David asked God never to let him be ashamed for trusting him.

Every true believer can come boldly to the throne of grace with the same plea.

Remember the gracious care of divine Providence from our birth and throughout infancy.

The One who has been our Help from birth should also be our Hope from youth.

We should not expect lasting ease or comfort from the world.

Those who love the Lord are often hated, persecuted or regarded as strange because of their convictions and conduct.

Yet God has always been their strong refuge.

His faithful servants may trust that he will not reject them in old age or forsake them when their strength declines.

Praising Christ's righteousness through old age (verses 14–24)

David resolved to speak about Christ's righteousness and the great salvation obtained through it.

This would occupy his speech not only on Sabbaths but on every day of the week, every year and throughout his life.

He would proclaim it not merely during appointed seasons of worship but on every occasion, all day long.

Why return so often to this subject? Because its riches cannot be counted.

Christ's righteousness is beyond expression, and the salvation it provides is everlasting.

God does not abandon his grey-haired servants when they can no longer work as they once did.

Indeed, he often strengthens their inner lives while their bodily strength declines.

Older disciples of Christ owe a testimony to those who come after them.

They should speak earnestly about the benefits of true religion, the certainty of God's promises and, especially, the Redeemer's everlasting righteousness.

With confidence in God's final deliverance, let us spend whatever days remain praising the Holy One of Israel with all our abilities.

While we tell of his righteousness and sing his praise, faith can lift us above fear and frailty and grant us foretastes of heaven's joy.

Above all the Lord's works, redemption deserves our praise.

The Lamb who was slain and redeemed us to God is worthy of every blessing and all thanksgiving.
classic_reading:
[Ps.71.1-Ps.71.13]
Chapter 71
Chapter Outline
Prayers that God would deliver and save. | (1-13) |
Believing praises. | (14-24) |
Verses 1-13
David prays that he might never be made ashamed of dependence upon God. With this petition every true believer may come boldly to the throne of grace. The gracious care of Divine providence in our birth and infancy, should engage us to early piety. He that was our Help from our birth, ought to be our Hope from our youth. Let none expect ease or comfort from the world. Those who love the Lord, often are hated and persecuted; men wondered at for their principles and conduct; but the Lord has been their strong refuge. The faithful servants of God may be assured that he will not cast them off in old age, nor forsake them when their strength fails.
[Ps.71.14-Ps.71.24]
Verses 14-24
The psalmist declares that the righteousness of Christ, and the great salvation obtained thereby, shall be the chosen subject of his discourse. Not on a sabbath only, but on every day of the week, of the year, of his life. Not merely at stated returns of solemn devotion, but on every occasion, all the day long. Why will he always dwell on this? Because he knew not the numbers thereof. It is impossible to measure the value or the fulness of these blessings. The righteousness is unspeakable, the salvation everlasting. God will not cast off his grey-headed servants when no longer capable of labouring as they have done. The Lord often strengthens his people in their souls, when nature is sinking into decay. And it is a debt which the old disciples of Christ owe to succeeding generations, to leave behind them a solemn testimony to the advantage of religion, and the truth of God's promises; and especially to the everlasting righteousness of the Redeemer. Assured of deliverance and victory, let us spend our days, while waiting the approach of death, in praising the Holy One of Israel with all our powers. And while speaking of his righteousness, and singing his praises, we shall rise above fears and infirmities, and have earnests of the joys of heaven. The work of redemption ought, above all God's works, to be spoken of by us in our praises. The Lamb that was slain, and has redeemed us to God, is worthy of all blessing and praise.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid begins with a prayer for Solomon.1He passes into a prophecy of the glories of his reign, and of Christ's kingdom.2–17Praise to God.18–20
David prays for Solomon (verse 1)

Part of this psalm concerns Solomon, but it belongs more fully and clearly to Christ.

Solomon was both a king and a king's son.

His godly father asked that God would give him wisdom, so that Solomon's reign might become a memorial and picture of the Messiah's kingdom.

This is a father's prayer for his child and a final blessing near the end of life.

The best thing parents can ask God to give their children is wisdom and grace to understand and fulfill their duties.

The Messiah's enduring kingdom (verses 2–17)

The psalm foretells the kingdom of Christ, and many of its promises cannot be fulfilled by Solomon.

At the beginning of Solomon's rule there were righteousness and peace.

But before his reign ended, trouble and injustice appeared.

The kingdom described here lasts as long as the sun, whereas Solomon's kingdom soon came to an end.

Henry adds that even Jewish interpreters understood it as speaking of the Messiah.

The glorious promises find their complete fulfillment only through Christ's reign.

Where his kingdom is established, discord and conflict diminish in families, churches and nations.

Christ's law written upon the heart makes people honest and just, willing to give each person what is owed and to live in love.

This produces abundant peace.

Holiness and love endure in his kingdom.

The world and human lives change constantly, but Christ's kingdom remains.

He descends through the grace and comfort of his Spirit like rain on freshly cut grass—on the living grass remaining to grow again, not on the pieces already cut off.

His gospel has been preached, or will be preached, to every nation.

Christ does not need human gifts or services, yet he deserves our best.

People who possess worldly wealth should use it to serve him and do good.

Prayer is offered through him and for his sake. Whatever we ask the Father, we should ask in Christ's name.

He is also worthy of praise, because our obligations to him are beyond measure.

Christ alone will be reverenced throughout the generations.

His name will be praised to the end of time and throughout eternity, and all nations will call him blessed.

Praise for redeeming love (verses 18–20)

We are taught to bless God in Christ, praising him for everything accomplished for us through his Son.

David earnestly prayed that the promise about the Messiah's kingdom would be fulfilled.

It is sad to see how little glory God receives from the world, although he is so generous toward it.

May we, like David, submit to Christ's authority and share in his righteousness and peace.

Let us bless God for the wonders of redeeming love.

May our days be spent—and our lives end—in prayer for the spread of Christ's gospel.
classic_reading:
[Ps.72.1]
Chapter 72
Chapter Outline
David begins with a prayer for Solomon. | (1) |
He passes into a prophecy of the glories of his reign, and of Christ's kingdom. | (2-17) |
Praise to God. | (18-20) |
Verse 1
This psalm belongs to Solomon in part, but to Christ more fully and clearly. Solomon was both the king and the king's son, and his pious father desired that the wisdom of God might be in him, that his reign might be a remembrance of the kingdom of the Messiah. It is the prayer of a father for his child; a dying blessing. The best we can ask of God for our children is, that God would give them wisdom and grace to know and to do their duty.
[Ps.72.2-Ps.72.17]
Verses 2-17
This is a prophecy of the kingdom of Christ; many passages in it cannot be applied to the reign of Solomon. There were righteousness and peace at first in the administration of his government; but, before the end of his reign, there were troubles and unrighteousness. The kingdom here spoken of is to last as long as the sun, but Solomon's was soon at an end. Even the Jewish expositors understood it of the kingdom of the Messiah. Observe many great and precious promises here made, which were to have full accomplishment only in the kingdom of Christ. As far as his kingdom is set up, discord and contentions cease, in families, churches, and nations. The law of Christ, written in the heart, disposes men to be honest and just, and to render to all their due; it likewise disposes men to live in love, and so produces abundance of peace. Holiness and love shall be lasting in Christ's kingdom. Through all the changes of the world, and all the changes of life, Christ's kingdom will support itself. And he shall, by the graces and comforts of his Spirit, come down like rain upon the mown grass; not on that cut down, but that which is left growing, that it may spring again. His gospel has been, or shall be, preached to all nations. Though he needs not the services of any, yet he must be served with the best. Those that have the wealth of this world, must serve Christ with it, do good with it. Prayer shall be made through him, or for his sake; whatever we ask of the Father, should be in his name. Praises shall be offered to him: we are under the highest obligations to him. Christ only shall be feared throughout all generations. To the end of time, and to eternity, his name shall be praised. All nations shall call HIM blessed.
[Ps.72.18-Ps.72.20]
Verses 18-20
We are taught to bless God in Christ, for all he has done for us by him. David is earnest in prayer for the fulfilment of this prophecy and promise. It is sad to think how empty the earth is of the glory of God, how little service and honour he has from a world to which he is so bountiful. May we, like David, submit to Christ's authority, and partake of his righteousness and peace. May we bless him for the wonders of redeeming love. May we spend our days, and end our lives, praying for the spread of his gospel.

The temptation to envy the wicked (verses 1–14)

The psalmist was strongly tempted to envy prosperous wicked people.

Many of God's faithful servants have faced the same testing.

He began, however, with an unshakable truth: God is good.

Remembering that goodness guards the mind against Satan's temptations.

Even strong believers can find their faith badly shaken. Some storms test the firmest anchors.

Foolish and wicked people sometimes enjoy great outward success and seem to escape many troubles.

They may live without fearing God and still become wealthy and influential.

Some remain relatively healthy until death and die without much pain, while godly people may spend their lives in illness and die with severe suffering.

Others experience no apparent terror when facing death.

But we cannot judge a person's state after death from the circumstances of that death.

These observations made God's people uncertain what to say, especially when their own suffering was bitter.

The psalmist spoke from real pain.

He felt tempted to believe that serving God had been pointless.

Yet genuine sanctification calls us to cleanse both soul and body from sin.

The heart is purified by Christ's blood received through faith and by the Holy Spirit beginning his work within.

That inward change appears outwardly in a heartfelt determination to pursue holiness and a blameless way of life.

Serving God and keeping his ordinances are never in vain.

The sanctuary reveals the end of the wicked (verses 15–20)

The psalmist restrained himself from speaking his harmful doubts to others.

He still respected God's people and did not want to injure their faith.

When we stop ourselves from giving voice to evil thoughts, that restraint may show genuine repentance for those thoughts.

Few things wound God's people more than hearing that serving the Lord is useless, because this contradicts their whole experience.

He prayed for understanding and came before God in the sanctuary.

There he considered the end toward which the wicked were moving.

They seemed secure at the height of prosperity, yet were preparing for ruin.

A suffering righteous person's troubles end in peace.

The wicked person's pleasures end in destruction.

Their prosperity is fleeting and precarious, like walking on slippery ground.

It is a show without substance, a shadow or a dream that appears pleasant during sleep but may itself disturb the sleeper.

Learning to draw nearer to God (verses 21–28)

God would not allow such a temptation if his grace were insufficient not merely to preserve his people, but also to make them spiritually richer through the trial.

Envy and discontent hurt the soul.

Looking back, the psalmist recognized his own folly and ignorance.

When good people fall into wrong thoughts, words or actions during intense temptation, they should afterward acknowledge them with sorrow and shame.

The credit for deliverance belongs not to our wisdom but to God's gracious presence and Christ's intercession.

Those committed to the Lord receive counsel from his word and Spirit, their best guides here.

Then he receives them into glory.

The hope of heaven can reconcile believers to dark and mysterious earthly Providence.

This experience drew the psalmist closer to God.

Even heaven would not make us happy without God's presence and love.

The world's beauty and splendor vanish.

Our bodies lose their strength through illness, age and death. When bodily strength fails, confidence and comfort often fail too.

But Jesus Christ offers to be everything needed by any poor sinner willing to renounce other final hopes.

Our sins have separated us from God.

A mere profession of Christ while we continue in deliberate sin only increases condemnation.

Let us therefore draw near and remain near through faith and prayer.

Those who sincerely trust the Lord always have reason to thank him.

Blessed Lord, since you have promised to be our portion in the coming world, keep us from choosing anything else as our portion here.
classic_reading:
[Ps.73.1-Ps.73.14]
Chapter 73
Chapter Outline
The psalmist's temptation. | (1-14) |
How he gained a victory over it. | (15-20) |
How he profited by it. | (21-28) |
Verses 1-14
The psalmist was strongly tempted to envy the prosperity of the wicked; a common temptation, which has tried the graces of many saints. But he lays down the great principle by which he resolved to abide. It is the goodness of God. This is a truth which cannot be shaken. Good thoughts of God will fortify against Satan's temptations. The faith even of strong believers may be sorely shaken, and ready to fail. There are storms that will try the firmest anchors. Foolish and wicked people have sometimes a great share of outward prosperity. They seem to have the least share of the troubles of this life; and they seem to have the greatest share of its comforts. They live without the fear of God, yet they prosper, and get on in the world. Wicked men often spend their lives without much sickness, and end them without great pain; while many godly persons scarcely know what health is, and die with great sufferings. Often the wicked are not frightened, either by the remembrance of their sins, or the prospect of their misery, but they die without terror. We cannot judge men's state beyond death, by what passes at their death. He looked abroad, and saw many of God's people greatly at a loss. Because the wicked are so very daring, therefore his people return hither; they know not what to say to it, and the rather, because they drink deep of the bitter cup of affliction. He spoke feelingly when he spoke of his own troubles; there is no disputing against sense, except by faith. From all this arose a strong temptation to cast off religion. But let us learn that the true course of sanctification consists in cleansing a man from all pollution both of soul and body. The heart is cleansed by the blood of Christ laid hold upon by faith; and by the begun works of the Lord's Spirit, manifested in the hearty resolution, purpose, and study of holiness, and a blameless course of life and actions, the hands are cleansed. It is not in vain to serve God and keep his ordinances.
[Ps.73.15-Ps.73.20]
Verses 15-20
The psalmist having shown the progress of his temptation, shows how faith and grace prevailed. He kept up respect for God's people, and with that he restrained himself from speaking what he had thought amiss. It is a sign that we repent of the evil thoughts of the heart, if we suppress them. Nothing gives more offence to God's children, than to say it is vain to serve God; for there is nothing more contrary to their universal experience. He prayed to God to make this matter plain to him; and he understood the wretched end of wicked people; even in the height of their prosperity they were but ripening for ruin. The sanctuary must be the resort of a tempted soul. The righteous man's afflictions end in peace, therefore he is happy; the wicked man's enjoyments end in destruction, therefore he is miserable. The prosperity of the wicked is short and uncertain, slippery places. See what their prosperity is; it is but a vain show, it is only a corrupt imagination, not substance, but a mere shadow; it is as a dream, which may please us a little while we are slumbering, yet even then it disturbs our repose.
[Ps.73.21-Ps.73.28]
Verses 21-28
God would not suffer his people to be tempted, if his grace were not sufficient, not only to save them from harm, but to make them gainers by it. This temptation, the working of envy and discontent, is very painful. In reflecting upon it, the psalmist owns it was his folly and ignorance thus to vex himself. If good men, at any time, through the surprise and strength of temptation, think, or speak, or act amiss, they will reflect upon it with sorrow and shame. We must ascribe our safety in temptation, and our victory, not to our own wisdom, but to the gracious presence of God with us, and Christ's intercession for us. All who commit themselves to God, shall be guided with the counsel both of his word and of his Spirit, the best counsellors here, and shall be received to his glory in another world; the believing hopes and prospects of which will reconcile us to all dark providences. And the psalmist was hereby quickened to cleave the closer to God. Heaven itself could not make us happy without the presence and love of our God. The world and all its glory vanishes. The body will fail by sickness, age, and death; when the flesh fails, the conduct, courage, and comfort fail. But Christ Jesus, our Lord, offers to be all in all to every poor sinner, who renounces all other portions and confidences. By sin we are all far from God. And a profession Christ, if we go on in sin, will increase our condemnation. May we draw near, and keep near, to our God, by faith and prayer, and find it good to do so. Those that with an upright heart put their trust in God, shall never want matter for thanksgiving to him. Blessed Lord, who hast so graciously promised to become our portion in the next world, prevent us from choosing any other in this.

Lament over a devastated sanctuary (verses 1–11)

Henry understands this psalm as appearing to describe the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by the Chaldeans.

The people of God laid their terrible situation before the Lord and left it in his hands.

They recalled what he had previously done for them.

If the deliverance from Egypt encouraged Israel to trust that God would not abandon his people, Christians have even stronger reason to believe he will not reject those redeemed through Christ's own blood.

Unbelievers and persecutors may silence faithful ministers, close places of worship and boast that they will destroy both God's people and their religion.

For a long time such schemes may appear successful.

The oppressed may see no possibility of escape.

Yet God preserves a remnant of believers, the seed of a future harvest.

The church that appears despised today has outlived many enemies who once celebrated victory over her.

When hostile power is most terrifying, take refuge in God's power through earnest prayer.

Remember the God of creation and covenant (verses 12–17)

The church turned from complaint to the memory of God's ancient works as her King.

What he had done before encouraged his people to trust him again.

These deliverances were his work, which no one else could have accomplished.

Remembering Providence strengthens faith and hope under present difficulties.

The God of Israel is also the God of nature.

He faithfully maintains the order of day and night.

He will likewise remain faithful to those he has chosen.

We have as much reason to expect affliction in this world as to expect night and winter.

But we have no more reason to despair of comfort's return than to despair that day and summer will return.

In the world to come these changes will finally disappear.

Prayer for the poor and oppressed (verses 18–23)

The psalmist asked God to defend his church against enemies.

The folly of those who despise his gospel and servants will become evident.

We should pray that he will enlighten nations living in darkness and rescue his people.

Then the poor and needy will have reason to praise his name.

Blessed Savior, you are the same yesterday, today and forever.

Make your people more than conquerors.

Be everything to them in every place and every circumstance, so that even your poor and afflicted servants will praise your name.
classic_reading:
[Ps.74.1-Ps.74.11]
Chapter 74
Chapter Outline
The desolations of the sanctuary. | (1-11) |
Pleas for encouraging faith. | (12-17) |
Petitions for deliverances. | (18-23) |
Verses 1-11
This psalm appears to describe the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by the Chaldeans. The deplorable case of the people of God, at the time, is spread before the Lord, and left with him. They plead the great things God had done for them. If the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt was encouragement to hope that he would not cast them off, much more reason have we to believe, that God will not cast off any whom Christ has redeemed with his own blood. Infidels and persecutors may silence faithful ministers, and shut up places of worship, and say they will destroy the people of God and their religion together. For a long time they may prosper in these attempts, and God's oppressed servants may see no prospect of deliverance; but there is a remnant of believers, the seed of a future harvest, and the despised church has survived those who once triumphed over her. When the power of enemies is most threatening, it is comfortable to flee to the power of God by earnest prayer.
[Ps.74.12-Ps.74.17]
Verses 12-17
The church silences her own complaints. What God had done for his people, as their King of old, encouraged them to depend on him. It was the Lord's doing, none besides could do it. This providence was food to faith and hope, to support and encourage in difficulties. The God of Israel is the God of nature. He that is faithful to his covenant about the day and the night, will never cast off those whom he has chosen. We have as much reason to expect affliction, as to expect night and winter. But we have no more reason to despair of the return of comfort, than to despair of day and summer. And in the world above we shall have no more changes.
[Ps.74.18-Ps.74.23]
Verses 18-23
The psalmist begs that God would appear for the church against their enemies. The folly of such as revile his gospel and his servants will be plain to all. Let us call upon our God to enlighten the dark nations of the earth; and to rescue his people, that the poor and needy may praise his name. Blessed Saviour, thou art the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever. Make thy people more than conquerors. Be thou, Lord, all in all to them in every situation and circumstances; for then thy poor and needy people will praise thy name.

Gratitude, justice and the rule of Christ (verses 1–5)

We often pray repeatedly when we are seeking mercy.

After receiving mercy, should we thank God only once or twice?

The Lord shows that he is near us through the blessings we seek from him.

Everyone entrusted with public responsibility must administer it with integrity and justice.

Henry understands these words as especially applicable to Christ and his government.

Human sin threatened the ruin of all creation, but Christ saved the world from complete destruction.

The One whom God has made our wisdom commands us to be wise.

He warns proud and defiant sinners not to boast of their power or persist in contempt for God.

Every hope humanity has for the present and every prospect of future happiness flows ultimately from the Son of God.

All judgment and promotion belong to God (verses 6–10)

No human cause, considered by itself, can bring people to positions of honor without the First Cause—God.

Advancement comes neither from the east, west nor south.

Henry notes the absence of the north: in the language of the source, the word for north can also refer to a hidden place, which leads him to relate promotion to the secret counsel of God.

From the Lord alone every person receives the final judgment appointed to them.

In the cup of affliction offered to God's people, mercy and grace are mixed with suffering.

For unrepentant wicked people, the same image points to a mixture of divine judgment.

God's people may experience the same public disasters as other people, but the dregs of the cup are reserved for those who remain in sin.

The exaltation of David's Son, Christ, will be the subject of everlasting praise among the saints.

Let sinners submit to the King of righteousness.

Let believers rejoice in him and obey his commands.
classic_reading:
[Ps.75.1-Ps.75.5]
Chapter 75
Chapter Outline
The psalmist declares his resolution of executing judgment. | (1-5) |
He rebukes the wicked, and concludes with resolutions to praise God. | (6-10) |
Verses 1-5
We often pray for mercy, when in pursuit of it; and shall we only once or twice give thanks, when we obtain it? God shows that he is nigh to us in what we call upon him for. Public trusts are to be managed uprightly. This may well be applied to Christ and his government. Man's sin threatened to destroy the whole creation; but Christ saved the world from utter ruin. He who is made of God to us wisdom, bids us be wise. To the proud, daring sinners he says, Boast not of your power, persist not in contempt. All the present hopes and future happiness of the human race spring from the Son of God.
[Ps.75.6-Ps.75.10]
Verses 6-10
No second causes will raise men to preferment without the First Cause. It comes neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. He mentions not the north; the same word that signifies the north, signifies the secret place; and from the secret of God's counsel it does come. From God alone all must receive their doom. There are mixtures of mercy and grace in the cup of affliction, when it is put into the hands of God's people; mixtures of the curse, when it is put into the hands of the wicked. God's people have their share in common calamities, but the dregs of the cup are for the wicked. The exaltation of the Son of David will be the subject of the saints' everlasting praises. Then let sinners submit to the King of righteousness, and let believers rejoice in and obey him.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist speaks of God's power.1–6All have to fear and to trust in him.7–12
God is known among his people (verses 1–6)

Happy is a people whose land is filled with the knowledge of God.

Happy, too, are individuals whose hearts are filled with that knowledge.

It is the glory and happiness of a nation to have God present through his appointed ordinances.

The enemies of God's church may act with great pride. But the Lord will demonstrate that he is greater than those opposing him.

See how powerful even God's rebuke can be.

Christians may read these words joyfully in view of the benefits bestowed upon them through the Redeemer.

Holy fear and confidence in God's justice (verses 7–12)

God's people are described as the meek of the earth—quiet and peaceable people who endure wrong but refuse to do wrong themselves.

The righteous Lord may seem silent for a long time. Eventually, however, he will make his judgment heard.

We live in an angry, provoking world.

Human rage often hurts us, and the anticipation of further harm may make us even more afraid.

But God sets limits to human anger.

Whatever will not ultimately serve his glory, he will prevent from coming to pass.

He restrains human wrath as he restrains the roaring sea: it may come this far, but no farther.

Everyone should therefore submit to him.

Our proper offerings are prayers, praise and above all our hearts.

God's name is glorious; he alone deserves our highest reverence.

The Lord can humble the proudest rulers with astonishing ease.

Henry compares the removal of a prince's courage to picking a flower from its stem or a cluster of grapes from its vine.

God can take away the boldness of the most defiant people.

Since no one can successfully contend against him, our wisdom and duty are to submit, seek his favor as our portion, and entrust all our concerns to his care.
classic_reading:
[Ps.76.1-Ps.76.6]
Chapter 76
Chapter Outline
The psalmist speaks of God's power. | (1-6) |
All have to fear and to trust in him. | (7-12) |
Verses 1-6
Happy people are those who have their land filled with the knowledge of God! happy persons that have their hearts filled with that knowledge! It is the glory and happiness of a people to have God among them by his ordinances. Wherein the enemies of the church deal proudly, it will appear that God is above them. See the power of God's rebukes. With pleasure may Christians apply this to the advantages bestowed by the Redeemer.
[Ps.76.7-Ps.76.12]
Verses 7-12
God's people are the meek of the earth, the quiet in the land, that suffer wrong, but do none. The righteous God seems to keep silence long, yet, sooner or later, he will make judgment to be heard. We live in an angry, provoking world; we often feel much, and are apt to fear more, from the wrath of man. What will not turn to his praise, shall not be suffered to break out. He can set bounds to the wrath of man, as he does to the raging sea; hitherto it shall come, and no further. Let all submit to God. Our prayers and praises, and especially our hearts, are the presents we should bring to the Lord. His name is glorious, and he is the proper object of our fear. He shall cut off the spirit of princes; he shall slip it off easily, as we slip off a flower from the stalk, or a bunch of grapes from the vine; so the word signifies. He can dispirit the most daring: since there is no contending with God, it is our wisdom, as it is our duty, to submit to him. Let us seek his favour as our portion, and commit all our concerns to him.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist's troubles and temptation.1–10He encourages himself by the remembrance of God's help of his people.11–20
Distress, prayer and dangerous conclusions (verses 1–10)

Days of trouble should be days of prayer.

When God seems to withdraw his presence, we must continue seeking him.

The psalmist did not look for a distraction in work or amusement. He sought God himself, his favor and his grace.

People troubled in spirit should pray, not merely brood over their distress.

The psalmist concentrated so much on suffering that his usual means of consolation increased his sorrow.

When he remembered God, his thoughts turned only to divine justice and anger.

His spirit felt overwhelmed.

Yet we should not let grief over comforts lost make us ungrateful for comforts that remain.

He tried to recall the promises and past mercies that had sustained him during earlier difficulties.

The words express the condition of a grieving soul that feels deserted and walks in darkness—a condition even believers may experience (Isaiah 50:10).

Few things wound a godly soul more deeply than the thought that God is angry with it.

During dark periods, Christians may be tempted to draw false conclusions about their own spiritual state and the future of God's church.

We must resist these thoughts.

Let Scripture answer the questions unbelief raises.

A troubled fountain may eventually clear again.

Remembering former times of comfort can encourage fresh hope and bring relief.

Such fears arise from weakness in faith.

Despair and distrust are too often weaknesses of believers during affliction.

When unbelief stirs within us, we should recognize it sorrowfully and suppress it.

Remembering God's works (verses 11–20)

The remembrance of God's works is a powerful remedy against distrust of his goodness and promises.

He is God and does not change.

His way is in the sanctuary.

We can be certain that everything he does is holy.

Nevertheless, his purposes are often like deep waters that cannot be sounded, or the course of a ship that leaves no trace.

God brought Israel out of Egypt.

This deliverance pictured the greater redemption accomplished in the fullness of time through Christ—both by the price he paid and by the power he exercises.

If we have entertained doubts about God's kindness, turn promptly to meditate on the One who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all.

How can we doubt that with Christ he will graciously give everything necessary for our salvation?

Verses 1-10
Days of trouble must be days of prayer; when God seems to have withdrawn from us, we must seek him till we find him. In the day of his trouble the psalmist did not seek for the diversion of business or amusement, but he sought God, and his favor and grace. Those that are under trouble of mind, must pray it away. He pored upon the trouble; the methods that should have relieved him did but increase his grief. When he remembered God, it was only the Divine justice and wrath. His spirit was overwhelmed, and sank under the load. But let not the remembrance of the comforts we have lost, make us unthankful for those that are left. Particularly he called to remembrance the comforts with which he supported himself in former sorrows. Here is the language of a sorrowful, deserted soul, walking in darkness; a common case even among those that fear the Lord, [Isa.50.10] Is 50:10. Nothing wounds and pierces like the thought of God's being angry. God's own people, in a cloudy and dark day, may be tempted to make wrong conclusions about their spiritual state, and that of God's kingdom in the world. But we must not give way to such fears. Let faith answer them from the Scripture. The troubled fountain will work itself clear again; and the recollection of former times of joyful experience often raises a hope, tending to relief. Doubts and fears proceed from the want and weakness of faith. Despondency and distrust under affliction, are too often the infirmities of believers, and, as such, are to be thought upon by us with sorrow and shame. When, unbelief is working in us, we must thus suppress its risings.
[Ps.77.11-Ps.77.20]
Verses 11-20
The remembrance of the works of God, will be a powerful remedy against distrust of his promise and goodness; for he is God, and changes not. God's way is in the sanctuary. We are sure that God is holy in all his works. God's ways are like the deep waters, which cannot be fathomed; like the way of a ship, which cannot be tracked. God brought Israel out of Egypt. This was typical of the great redemption to be wrought out in the fulness of time, both by price and power. If we have harboured doubtful thoughts, we should, without delay, turn our minds to meditate on that God, who spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, that with him, he might freely give us all things.

Scripture and the duty to teach children (verses 1–8)

The teachings in this psalm are called deep or dark sayings because they deserve careful examination.

God's law was given with an express command that parents should teach it diligently to their children, so that God's people would continue serving him through future generations.

The record of his providential dealings—both mercy and judgment—should help children recognize God's will and obey it.

Remembering his mighty works strengthens our resolve to keep his commandments.

Hypocrisy opens a broad road toward apostasy.

People whose hearts are not rightly devoted to God will not remain faithful.

Negligent or wicked parents may be responsible for the spiritual destruction of their children.

Young people must honor their parents and obey everything that is lawful.

But they must not obey commands requiring sin or imitate evil parental examples.

Israel's repeated unbelief (verses 9–39)

Sin drains courage and weakens the heart.

Forgetting God's works causes disobedience to his commands.

The history of Israel displays a long conflict between divine goodness and human wickedness.

God hears people's complaining and distrust and is greatly displeased with it.

Those who will not trust his merciful power may come to experience his righteous judgment.

We cannot claim to trust God for eternal salvation while consistently refusing to trust his Providence along the way.

He opens heaven's door to those who ask, seek and knock through faith and prayer.

Our distrust, therefore, aggravates our sins.

God sometimes punished Israel not by refusing their sinful cravings but by granting what they demanded.

Unrestrained desires never become satisfied.

Those who indulge a lust do not thereby escape it.

Hard indeed are hearts that neither divine kindness melts nor divine judgment breaks.

People who persist in sin should expect continuing trouble.

Our own lives are often joyless and unproductive because we do not live by faith.

Under correction, Israel sometimes professed repentance.

But their conduct soon showed their insincerity and lack of perseverance.

Israel's history reflects the condition of our own hearts and lives.

Its record also resembles the history of nations and churches, which often ignore both divine mercy and judgment until wrongdoing reaches its full measure.

Great spiritual privileges have not always kept even churches faithful to God's word.

True believers also acknowledge years in which they abused Providence's kindness.

When they enter heaven, they will marvel at God's patience and mercy in bringing them there.

Wilderness guidance and settlement (verses 40–55)

Receiving divine mercy should never make us feel free to sin.

That misuse of mercy may bring judgment closer.

But people corrected for sin should not become discouraged from repentance.

The Holy One of Israel acts for his own glory and for the ultimate good of his people.

When Israel forgot his previous favors, it began to limit God in its expectations for the future.

God led his people out like a flock of sheep and guided them through the wilderness with the tenderness and care of a shepherd.

So Jesus, the true Joshua, leads his church through the spiritual wilderness.

No earthly Canaan and no worldly advantage should make believers forget that the church remains in a wilderness during this life.

A far more glorious rest is still reserved for God's people.

God's mercy despite continued ingratitude (verses 56–72)

Once Israel settled in Canaan, the children repeated their parents' sins.

Though God gave them his testimony, they turned away.

Deliberate sin among people bearing God's name insults his holiness and exposes them to his justice.

Those whom the Lord abandons become easy prey to destructive enemies.

Yet sooner or later he also brings disgrace upon the enemies of his people.

He gave Israel good government through a king after his own heart.

Henry sees this final act of divine favor as the climax of the psalm.

David pictured Christ, the great and good Shepherd.

Christ was first humbled and afterward exalted.

He is filled with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and his subjects may trust both the uprightness of his heart and the skill of his hands.

His government and peace will have no end.

Every test of human nature confirms the Bible's warning that the heart is deeply deceitful and corrupt.

Only being recreated by the Holy Spirit can cure human ungodliness.

Verses 1-8
These are called dark and deep sayings, because they are carefully to be looked into. The law of God was given with a particular charge to teach it diligently to their children, that the church may abide for ever. Also, that the providences of God, both in mercy and in judgment, might encourage them to conform to the will of God. The works of God much strengthen our resolution to keep his commandments. Hypocrisy is the high road to apostacy; those that do not set their hearts right, will not be stedfast with God. Many parents, by negligence and wickedness, become murderers of their children. But young persons, though they are bound to submit in all things lawful, must not obey sinful orders, or copy sinful examples.
[Ps.78.9-Ps.78.39]
Verses 9-39
Sin dispirits men, and takes away the heart. Forgetfulness of God's works is the cause of disobedience to his laws. This narrative relates a struggle between God's goodness and man's badness. The Lord hears all our murmurings and distrusts, and is much displeased. Those that will not believe the power of God's mercy, shall feel the fire of his indignation. Those cannot be said to trust in God's salvation as their happiness at last, who can not trust his providence in the way to it. To all that by faith and prayer, ask, seek, and knock, these doors of heaven shall at any time be opened; and our distrust of God is a great aggravation of our sins. He expressed his resentment of their provocation; not in denying what they sinfully lusted after, but in granting it to them. Lust is contented with nothing. Those that indulge their lust, will never be estranged from it. Those hearts are hard indeed, that will neither be melted by the mercies of the Lord, nor broken by his judgments. Those that sin still, must expect to be in trouble still. And the reason why we live with so little comfort, and to so little purpose, is, because we do not live by faith. Under these rebukes they professed repentance, but they were not sincere, for they were not constant. In Israel's history we have a picture of our own hearts and lives. God's patience, and warnings, and mercies, imbolden them to harden their hearts against his word. And the history of kingdoms is much the same. Judgments and mercies have been little attended to, until the measure of their sins has been full. And higher advantages have not kept churches from declining from the commandments of God. Even true believers recollect, that for many a year they abused the kindness of Providence. When they come to heaven, how will they admire the Lord's patience and mercy in bringing them to his kingdom!
[Ps.78.40-Ps.78.55]
Verses 40-55
Let not those that receive mercy from God, be thereby made bold to sin, for the mercies they receive will hasten its punishment; yet let not those who are under Divine rebukes for sin, be discouraged from repentance. The Holy One of Israel will do what is most for his own glory, and what is most for their good. Their forgetting former favours, led them to limit God for the future. God made his own people to go forth like sheep; and guided them in the wilderness, as a shepherd his flock, with all care and tenderness. Thus the true Joshua, even Jesus, brings his church out of the wilderness; but no earthly Canaan, no worldly advantages, should make us forget that the church is in the wilderness while in this world, and that there remaineth a far more glorious rest for the people of God.
[Ps.78.56-Ps.78.72]
Verses 56-72
After the Israelites were settled in Canaan, the children were like their fathers. God gave them his testimonies, but they turned back. Presumptuous sins render even Israelites hateful to God's holiness, and exposed to his justice. Those whom the Lord forsakes become an easy prey to the destroyer. And sooner or later, God will disgrace his enemies. He set a good government over his people; a monarch after his own heart. With good reason does the psalmist make this finishing, crowning instance of God's favour to Israel; for David was a type of Christ, the great and good Shepherd, who was humbled first, and then exalted; and of whom it was foretold, that he should be filled with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding. On the uprightness of his heart, and the skilfulness of his hands, all his subjects may rely; and of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end. Every trial of human nature hitherto, confirms the testimony of Scripture, that the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked, and nothing but being created anew by the Holy Ghost can cure the ungodliness of any.

A devastated holy city (verses 1–5)

God's people brought their distress before him.

Where else could children go but to their Father, who is able and willing to help?

Sin had brought a dreadful change upon the holy city.

The people themselves defiled it through wrongdoing, and God permitted their enemies to defile it through violence and contempt.

They longed for reconciliation with him.

People who regard God's favor as better than life naturally dread his displeasure as worse than death.

Whenever we suffer, we should first beg the Lord to cleanse away the guilt of sin.

Then we can look for the comfort of his tender mercy.

A plea grounded in God's mercy (verses 6–13)

Those who continually ignore God and refuse to pray show that they do not know him rightly.

However unrighteous the invaders' actions were, the Lord was righteous in permitting those events within his Providence.

Deliverance from trouble becomes a genuine mercy when it rests upon forgiveness of sin.

We should therefore pray even more earnestly for sin to be removed than for suffering to end.

The people claimed no merit before God.

Their only hope was his mercy.

They appealed to the glory of his name: Help and pardon us for your name's sake.

Christians should remember that they too may be bound by chains of sin.

The world can resemble a prison, and every person lives under a sentence of death whose execution may come suddenly.

How earnestly should we pray that the sighing of prisoners reaches God, and that he preserves those appointed to die!

What a glorious day it will be when the church, victorious over sin and sorrow, sees every spiritual enemy finally disarmed!

Then, generation after generation, the redeemed will praise their great Shepherd, Bishop, King and God.

God is complained to: whither should children go but to a Father able and willing to help them? See what a change sin made in the holy city, when the heathen were suffered to pour in upon them. God's own people defiled it by their sins, therefore he suffered their enemies to defile it by their insolence. They desired that God would be reconciled. Those who desire God's favour as better than life, cannot but dread his wrath as worse than death. In every affliction we should first beseech the Lord to cleanse away the guilt of our sins; then he will visit us with his tender mercies.
[Ps.79.6-Ps.79.13]
Verses 6-13
Those who persist in ignorance of God, and neglect of prayer, are the ungodly. How unrighteous soever men were, the Lord was righteous in permitting them to do what they did. Deliverances from trouble are mercies indeed, when grounded upon the pardon of sin; we should therefore be more earnest in prayer for the removal of our sins than for the removal of afflictions. They had no hopes but from God's mercies, his tender mercies. They plead no merit, they pretend to none, but, Help us for the glory of thy name; pardon us for thy name's sake. The Christian forgets not that he is often bound in the chain of his sins. The world to him is a prison; sentence of death is passed upon him, and he knows not how soon it may be executed. How fervently should he at all times pray, O let the sighing of a prisoner come before thee, according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou those that are appointed to die! How glorious will the day be, when, triumphant over sin and sorrow, the church beholds the adversary disarmed for ever! while that church shall, from age to age, sing the praises of her great Shepherd and Bishop, her King and her God.

A cry to the Shepherd of Israel (verses 1–7)

The One who dwells upon the mercy seat is the good Shepherd of his people.

Yet we cannot enjoy the consolation of his love or expect the protection of his mighty arm unless we receive his converting grace.

When the Lord seems displeased even with his people's prayers, several explanations may apply.

Their aims in praying may be wrong.

They may be secretly indulging a cherished sin.

Or he may be testing their patience and perseverance in prayer.

When God is displeased, his people may weep while their enemies rejoice.

Every salvation comes from his favor; no true conversion takes place apart from his grace.

The vine planted and cared for by God (verses 8–16)

The church is pictured as a vine and a vineyard.

Christ is the root; believers are the branches.

A vine is weak and needs support, yet it can spread widely and produce abundant fruit.

But if it produces no fruit, hardly any tree is so useless.

Have we not been planted in a carefully tended garden with every opportunity to bear the fruits of righteousness?

Yet empty leaves of religious profession and barren branches of doctrinal talk and ceremonial form often far outnumber genuine godliness.

The vineyard had been ruined.

There was a righteous reason for the change in God's dealings with his people.

Our condition is good or bad according to whether his favor rests upon us.

When we observe even the most faithful part of the visible church, we should not be surprised if God sends severe correction.

The psalm calls upon God to protect and restore the vine.

Lord, you formed this vineyard for yourself, so we may humbly commit its care to you.

The Man at God's right hand (verses 17–19)

The Messiah, Protector and Savior of the church, is the Man at God's right hand, the Arm of the Lord, to whom all authority has been given.

Through him we receive the strength to persevere to the end.

The vine cannot finally be destroyed, and no genuinely fruitful branch will perish.

But barren branches will be cut off and thrown into the fire.

We were redeemed so that we might serve the One who redeemed us, not return to the sins from which he rescued us.

He that dwelleth upon the mercy-seat, is the good Shepherd of his people. But we can neither expect the comfort of his love, nor the protection of his arm, unless we partake of his converting grace. If he is really angry at the prayers of his people, it is because, although they pray, their ends are not right, or there is some secret sin indulged in them, or he will try their patience and perseverance in prayer. When God is displeased with his people, we must expect to see them in tears, and their enemies in triumph. There is no salvation but from God's favour; there is no conversion to God but by his own grace.
[Ps.80.8-Ps.80.16]
Verses 8-16
The church is represented as a vine and a vineyard. The root of this vine is Christ, the branches are believers. The church is like a vine, needing support, but spreading and fruitful. If a vine do not bring forth fruit, no tree is so worthless. And are not we planted as in a well-cultivated garden, with every means of being fruitful in works of righteousness? But the useless leaves of profession, and the empty boughs of notions and forms, abound far more than real piety. It was wasted and ruined. There was a good reason for this change in God's way toward them. And it is well or ill with us, according as we are under God's smiles or frowns. When we consider the state of the purest part of the visible church, we cannot wonder that it is visited with sharp corrections. They request that God would help the vine. Lord, it is formed by thyself, and for thyself, therefore it may, with humble confidence, be committed to thyself.
[Ps.80.17-Ps.80.19]
Verses 17-19
The Messiah, the Protector and Saviour of the church, is the Man of God's right hand; he is the Arm of the Lord, for all power is given to him. In him is our strength, by which we are enabled to persevere to the end. The vine, therefore, cannot be ruined, nor can any fruitful branch perish; but the unfruitful will be cut off and cast into the fire. The end of our redemption is, that we should serve Him who hath redeemed us, and not go back to our old sins.
